why: No harness sends anything off the machine, and wiring a hook to ntfy/Pushover is a real (if known) project a normal user will not do. Genuinely changes behaviour: you leave the room instead of babysitting. Discounted slightly because vendors shipping mobile push within a year is plausible.

Briefing is explicit that nothing distinguishes wedged from productive; telling them apart by hand means watching one pane over minutes, which nobody does across 8 sessions. Impact real (recovers wasted hours) but capped because the signal is heuristic and a few false positives train the user to ignore it.

Spotting that you have hand-run the same procedure five times needs history correlated across sessions and weeks, which no harness retains and no user reconstructs. But this is the classic case of information not changing behaviour: authoring a skill is a real chunk of work, and a nudge saying you could rarely converts.

Subagent activity scrolls past in the owning pane, so it is visible-if-you-look rather than hidden; the workflow-stage half only exists for people already running Spacedock, a narrow slice. Tripwire could catch a bad stage but the audience and the frequency are both small.

No harness keeps queryable cross-session history, so counts and streaks are genuinely unreachable by hand. Also genuinely useless: the item itself concedes no decision is attached. Streaks are vanity telemetry and no action follows from them.

Claude /usage reports the weekly window in one command, and a Barista-style status line puts it on screen unprompted, so this is close to commodity already. Weekly pacing does shift model choice and when you start a big job, but it is a soft weekly nudge rather than a decision made often.

Read as an action: Claude ships Notification and SessionEnd hooks, so a competent user could wire a state-change alert in an afternoon, but they have not and other harnesses give them nothing. Replacing polling with being told is one of the few changes that measurably alters minute-to-minute behaviour.

git status is one command in a place the user knows; the only real cost is remembering to run it in each of several repos after sessions end. Impact overstated by the framing: uncommitted work sits in the working tree and does not evaporate, so actual loss needs a branch switch or worktree nuke and is rare.

Requires forward ETAs for every live session simultaneously, and no harness estimates turn duration at all, so unobtainable by hand. But the promise is a prediction about agents that block unpredictably; one wrong all-clear and the user stops trusting it, and a push notification solves the same problem more robustly.

Quota is shown as a spot figure only; projecting it means sampling /usage twice, timing it, and doing arithmetic, which nobody does reliably. Knowing you hit the wall in 40 minutes genuinely changes a decision (drop to Sonnet, defer the long job) and does so on a regular basis.
